body.text: Jason Arday was appointed professor of sociology of education at the University of Cambridge in February 2023, becoming, at 37, the youngest Black person ever appointed to a professorship at the university. The appointment was widely celebrated across British academia as evidence of institutional progress, in a sector where Black professors remain starkly underrepresented. In 2024-25, Black academics accounted for just 1 per cent of professors in UK higher education.

In July 2026, allegations of plagiarism, questions about his research and disputes over claims in his biography triggered a wave of media investigations into his work and public account of his life. Cambridge subsequently announced an investigation into his academic qualifications and honorary appointments, alongside existing complaints concerning academic misconduct. Arday resigned on August 5, days after the scrutiny intensified, saying his resignation should not be “mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me”.

Nine days later, he was found unresponsive at his home in Battersea and pronounced dead, aged 41. An inquest subsequently opened after the coroner said there was reason to suspect an unnatural death. The inquest has been adjourned.

His case became a cultural battlefield over race, merit, diversity, representation and affirmative action. His exceptional visibility as Cambridge’s youngest Black professor was celebrated in British academia as evidence of institutional progress. At the same time, we need to think about how paradoxically intriguing his whole controversy was: the same visibility that was being celebrated made him disproportionately vulnerable to scrutiny and ideological attack.

There lies a substantial danger when institutions treat the presence of a marginalised individual as evidence that inequality has been overcome; representation might become a spectacle rather than transformation. Arday’s case asks for a rethink in the narrative of representation as inclusivity. There is a need to distinguish between representation as structural justice, when communities historically discriminated against demand the spaces they were never allowed to participate in, and representation as institutional tokenism, where a marginalised person is allowed to participate in an institution for the sake of inclusivity.

The excessive publicity surrounding his appointment itself illustrates a paradox: he was simultaneously recognised and othered. He was simply not allowed to be a scholar; he became a symbol of diversity, resilience, and institutional liberalism.
Ghettoisation through representation

Many fail to see the underlying consequences such identity politics might produce and, in Arday’s case, the consequences explicitly came to the surface. It could be understood as “ghettoisation through representation”, where once an individual from a marginalised community becomes a symbol, their individuality is rendered secondary to the political function they perform for the institution. What happens when such individuals get to exercise their own agency within this contemporary diversity politics? Do they remain only as representatives of diversity? Identity politics cannot be dismissed altogether on account of such questions.

Asserting one’s identity through identity politics does not explicitly mean ghettoisation; in fact, identities which are “invisible” or have been historically invisibilised could utilise the very identity politics as a form of assertion. But the larger critique should ask whether mere institutional representation can be considered emancipation in itself. Do marginalised individuals still get to practise their agency via inclusive or diverse safeguards? Perhaps it’s intriguing to think that ghettoisation might not always occur through exclusion; sometimes, paradoxically, it occurs through inclusion itself.

The Dalit scholar becomes the “Dalit academic”; the Black professor becomes the “Black success story”; the disabled student becomes an inspirational narrative. Their intellectual identity is constantly subordinated to their social identity. They are made hypervisible as members of a community but not recognised as autonomous intellectuals.

This produces a peculiar form of institutional violence. The privileged individual is allowed the luxury of being mediocre, complex, contradictory, or simply ordinary, but the marginalised individual must constantly justify their presence. Their failure is never merely individual; it is made representative of the supposed inadequacy of their entire community. Nobody would argue that the existence of a corrupt uppered-caste* professor proves that uppered castes are incapable of academic excellence, yet the failure of one reserved-category candidate is routinely mobilised as evidence against reservation itself. Such individuals, therefore, are denied the right to individual failure; they are simply not allowed the luxury of failure. Their failure is projected as an incapacity produced by the very communities they belong to. Affirmative action and representative politics carry this political violence within them, but the problem is not representation itself; it is the politics surrounding it, be it left wing or right wing.
The Right and Left: two languages of victimisation

The political Right attacks affirmative action through the language of meritocracy. It portrays reservation as an undeserved privilege and an assault on excellence. But this conception of merit deliberately forgets history: merit is never produced in a social vacuum. Who attends better schools? Who has educated parents? Who is surrounded by professional networks and intergenerational familiarity with universities? Such questions reveal who decides merit. Caste and racial privileges become invisible in the heap of merit.

This is where an Ambedkarite intervention becomes particularly necessary. B.R. Ambedkar, the anti-caste reformer and principal architect of India’s Constitution, demanded separate electorates for the Depressed Classes, the term then used for communities now broadly identified as Dalits. The British government’s Communal Award of 1932 granted separate electorates, but the Poona Pact of September 1932 replaced them with reserved seats within joint electorates.

It is crucial to understand that Ambedkar considered reservation a teleological tool, meaning a means directed towards a larger end, that would change the lives of Dalits in India, but he never considered it an emancipatory tool in itself.

Perhaps this is precisely why the same critique needs extending to the liberal Left. The political Left should not be treated as automatically emancipatory. Liberal and Left institutions often celebrate representation while refusing to transform their own internal structures. They celebrate the marginalised as evidence, or a token, of their own progress but grow uncomfortable when the same individual challenges their institutional power and hegemony.

Institutional discrimination does not simply vanish because a progressive Left politician comes to power. In India, we cannot forget the case of Chuni Kotal, an Adivasi woman of the Lodha community of West Bengal. She died by suicide in 1992 after years of alleged caste-based discrimination and harassment at Vidyasagar University. An inquiry committee examining allegations against a university professor found that Kotal’s allegations of psychological torture based on her Lodha identity were prima facie correct, though a subsequent Ganguly Commission did not hold the professor responsible for her death.

She belonged to a community historically classified as a “criminal tribe” under British rule, a colonial classification whose stigma continued to affect the Lodha community after Independence. This occurred during Left Front rule in West Bengal, a CPI(M)-led coalition that governed the state from 1977 to 2011. Despite more than a decade in office by then, the Left Front failed to protect the marginalised or forcefully implement anti-caste measures in the state.

Her death became a devastating reminder that a government rhetorically committed to class equality could still fail to adequately confront caste and tribal hierarchies embedded within institutions. The ideological and material gap between class and caste politics speaks for itself. Caste cannot be treated as secondary to class. It did not emerge with capitalism; it attached itself to capitalism. It entered universities, bureaucracies, labour markets, housing, marriages, intellectual networks, and even supposedly progressive organisations. Most importantly, the Ambedkarite movement should not have to dissolve itself into a “universal revolution” to be considered politically legitimate.

The Khairlanji massacre of 2006 offers another devastating illustration among many others: the Maharashtra government of the time, a Congress-Nationalist Congress Party coalition, initially faced severe criticism over its handling of the killings and the police investigation. The state later ordered a CBI investigation and dismissed five policemen over alleged lapses in the investigation. The Maharashtra State Human Rights Commission also took suo motu cognisance of the case.

This reveals a disturbing pattern that remains equally prevalent under right-wing governance: Dalits are politically visible as voters but socially invisible as victims of structural violence. It needs to be acknowledged that the right wing in India has done tremendous political violence against the marginalised, but the Left and the political centre were equally no less culpable.

Ironically, the same pattern could be observed in Jason Arday’s case: he became a victim of both the Left and Right. The Right criticised diversity-hiring practices and questioned their capacity to hire meritorious individuals in British academia, while the Left seemed to have celebrated him as a success story, provided his presence “improved their moral image”. Both positions are forms of domination. The first excludes marginalised communities explicitly, and the second incorporates them selectively and symbolically. This is why representation without redistribution and institutional transformation can become another form of ghettoisation. Clustering such communities into identity categories, diversity committees, or specialised departments is a form of positive discrimination that needs critical reflection, especially when the fundamental structures of power remain untouched. A genuinely radical politics must therefore criticise both right-wing exclusion and liberal tokenism.
Beyond representation: an Ambedkarite perspective

Reservation is not just affirmative action; its foundation lies in representation within the structures of power. Ambedkar knew the caste monopoly well enough to recognise that formal equality in this nation would be insufficient. He writes in his book What Congress and Gandhi Have Done to the Untouchables (1945) that “the reservations demanded by the servile classes are really controls over the power of the governing classes.” For him, the idea behind reservation was a political safeguard against the concentration of power by dominant groups. The demand for reservation came after the demand for separate electorates, which was more radical in its conception of political representation.
It is crucial to note that reservation is not an exception to merit but a challenge to the caste monopoly over defining merit itself.

And this is where the question of going beyond representation arises. There persists a recurring issue that needs to be considered: affirmative action in India is disproportionately concentrated around higher education and employment. We often ignore the profoundly unequal educational journey that precedes the entrance examination. A Dalit or Adivasi student who reaches university has already survived an unequal societal structure. Reservation at the university entrance stage can partially correct exclusion, but can it compensate for unequal childhoods? Affirmative action must therefore move towards compensatory access, towards equity and developmental equality starting from schools. This should be done to produce dignified subjects with their own agency. The ultimate danger of contemporary diversity politics is that it mistakes visibility for equality. Institutions understand representation but are reluctant to redistribute power.

The Ambedkarite question is therefore more radical: Who owns knowledge? Who defines merit? Who controls institutions? Who gets to fail without their community being blamed? And who must constantly prove that they deserve to exist within spaces historically designed to exclude them?

Arday’s case should not be used either to defend affirmative action or to delegitimise it. Rather, it should force a more sophisticated critique. We must defend affirmative action precisely while criticising the tokenistic institutional mechanisms through which representation is often implemented. The answer to tokenism is not less representation or its abolition. The answer is deeper, structural transformation. For Ambedkar, education was not simply about social mobility; it was an instrument of emancipation. But emancipation cannot be restricted to allowing a few marginalised students to enter institutions while leaving the foundations of those very institutions intact—foundations that include the historical and epistemic violence done by delegitimising their knowledge production and their capacity as epistemic agents.

And perhaps this is the most important lesson for India: reservation must remain, but the struggle cannot end there. If caste inequality begins in childhood, affirmative action must begin there too. What is required, then, is not a political Left or a liberal centre but a radical Ambedkarite politics grounded in dignity, redistribution, and the annihilation of graded inequalities. One Dalit Vice Chancellor cannot dismantle Brahmanical institutional culture. One Dalit President cannot democratise the state. One Dalit professor cannot alone transform an overwhelmingly exclusionary academy. While mainstream parties ask marginalised communities to participate in an existing system, Ambedkarite politics asks whether the existing system itself can be democratised. Can the marginalised acquire the power to redefine the structures of power? The future of emancipatory politics for all oppressed communities cannot lie comfortably within the exhausted binary of Left and Right. It requires an autonomous political imagination capable of rethinking dignity and power.
*The term “uppered caste” is a deliberate linguistic term used by scholars and activists to show that social dominance is a constructed, historical position rather than an inherent status.
